Our only competitor, Jack Stirling Wakeley, was known to have been doing some very hard training, and after maintaining an almost even pace throughout the 24 hours, won by the huge margin of 10 miles, having covered the distance of 122 miles 1,411 yards.

These included Charlie Churcher, who developed leg trouble, Pat Sapcote, Fred Herring, Jack Wakeley and Don Heath, so that by the end of the race we had just a bare four left, who finished in fourth position, 2 points behind Woodford.

At half distance we had a four point lead, with the “ A ” team scoring: Jack Rutland 2, Jack Bidgood 4, Jack Wakeley 9, Bert Clayton was close behind but was having an off day owing to a badly bruised heel.

Jack Bidgood started going up towards the front quite early with Jack Wakeley and Jack Rutland not too far back. Then there followed all in quick succession the remaining five of the “ A ” Team, Don Heath, Hugh McGreechan, “Sir” Harry Shields, Joe Wilson and Dick Frazer.

Jack Stirling Wakeley and Jack Rutland finished 4th and 5th in the Hastings—Brighton Walk on August 19th and Jack Wakeley was 3rd in the handicap.

Dismayed, but not beaten, our whipper went back to the hero of the race, Jack Wakeley, walking in the 36th position. Learning of our bad luck and listening to the entreaties and bullyings of the said whip, Jack put in a superhuman effort and caught nine men in the last three-quarters of a mile.
Jack Wakeley hovered about 30th position until half the distance had been covered, after which he improved his position at a steady rate, gaining about 15 places in the last 15 miles to finish 11th.

In winning this race, Jack Stirling Wakeley also won the " Tommy Green " Cup for the Best Belgrave Athlete of the Year. Jack led throughout and finished a comfortable winner from a big and classy field of notable distance walkers.
Close behind were Jack Rutland, Jack Bidgood, Jack Wakeley and Harry Shields. As early as Croydon, Jack Wakeley showed signs of trouble with his shoes and soon began losing ground.

It was then that Harry Shields and Jack Wakeley started putting in some good work, and on a further check at 20 miles we found that Woodford had a comfortable lead of 20 points over Poly, whilst Leicester had dropped to third place with us still fourth.
Our fourth man, Jack Wakeley, was not far away, but making a check at half distance, it looked almost impossible for us to be placed, whilst there seemed no doubt that Poly would take team honours.
Among the 10,000 participants in the Annual International Four Days' Marches held at Nijmegen, Holland, from July 22nd to 26th, were six Belgravians; one—Jack Wakeley—in the R.W.A.

Since our last issue, Jack Stirling Wakeley was taken suddenly ill and had to be rushed to hospital for an operation. We are pleased to report that he is now fully recovered and hopes to be out training again soon.

However Jack Wakeley who had only intended making it a stroll, being his first long walk following his operation, made a great effort to push through and finish as our fourth man to make us second in the team race, only five points behind the winners.
In the early stages, Jack Bidgood Bert Clayton, Jack Baker, Jack Wakeley and George Oliver, walked in a group with Don Heath and Joe Wilson not far away.
